extracted.intended_audience: scientists, journal editors, science journalists, and general readers interested in research ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and reporting conflicts of interest (financial and non-financial) by psychologists and how those disclosures (or lack thereof) should appear in research outputs and related publicity. Focus is on transparency about paid speaking, consulting, business interests and prominence that could influence research interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of paid speaking/consulting earnings in research papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Some star psychologists don’t disclose in research papers the large sums they earn for talking about their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should disclose substantial payments received for public speaking or consulting that relate to the topic of their research. Omission of large sums earned for promoting or discussing one’s work in public forums is presented as a potential concern because it can create an appearance (or reality) of bias that readers and reviewers should be able to assess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of consulting businesses and commercial advisory roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: the researcher started a business, iGen Consulting, “to advise companies and organizations on generational differences based on her expertise and research on the topic”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers must declare advisory or commercial enterprises that draw on their scholarly expertise and could financially benefit from research outcomes. The description should include the nature of the business, whom it advises, and how it connects to the published work so that potential conflicts are clear to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of non‑financial conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Related coverage notes that Nature journals have tightened rules on non-financial conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-financial conflicts — such as professional prominence, advocacy, coinage/branding of concepts, close ties to advocacy groups, or substantial media presence — should be disclosed where policies require, because they can influence interpretation and promotion of findings even absent direct payments. Journals may have specific rules requiring disclosure of these roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about self-promotion, branding or coinage tied to research
rubrics_metrics.description: The researcher 'calls them the ‘iGen’ generation, a name she says she coined' and markets that expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an author has created a brand, coined a term, or actively promotes a concept commercially tied to their research, that linkage should be transparent. Disclosure helps readers judge whether promotional incentives might affect study framing, interpretation, or claims made in the paper and related publicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of whether undisclosed interests affect credibility and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The article asks: 'Is that a concern?' regarding undisclosed earnings and prominence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators (editors, reviewers, readers) should assess whether undisclosed financial or non-financial interests plausibly bias study design, analysis, interpretation, or public communication. Even if not provably biasing the data, undisclosed interests can undermine trust and should be weighed when interpreting claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with journal conflict-of-interest policies and their tightening
rubrics_metrics.description: Related articles and site links reference journals tightening rules on non-financial conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must follow the COI disclosure requirements of the journal (including any expanded requirements for non-financial interests). Editors should enforce these policies and update them as necessary; reviewers and readers should expect and check for compliance. Failure to comply can prompt corrections, editorials, or policy changes.
